sections.title: 英语知识运用
sections.directions: Directions: Read the following text. Choose the best word(s) for each numbered blank and mark A, B, C or D on the ANSWER SHEET. (10 points)

blocks.content: Many theories concerning the causes of juvenile delinquency (crimes committed by young people) focus either on the individual or on society as the major contributing influence. Theories
on the individual suggest that children engage in criminal behavior
they were not sufficiently penalized for previous misdeeds or that they have learned criminal behavior through
with others. Theories focusing on the role of society suggest that children commit crimes in
to their failure to rise above their socioeconomic status,
as a rejection of middle-class values. Most theories of juvenile delinquency have focused on children from disadvantaged families,
the fact that children from wealthy homes also commit crimes. The latter may commit crimes
lack of adequate parental control. All theories, however, are tentative and are
to criticism. Changes in the social structure may indirectly
juvenile crime rates. For example, changes in the economy that
to fewer job opportunities for youth and rising unemployment
make gainful employment increasingly difficult to obtain. The resulting discontent may in
lead more youths into criminal behavior. Families have also
changes these years. More families consist of one-parent households or two working parents;
, children are likely to have less supervision at home
was common in the traditional family
. This lack of parental supervision is thought to be an influence on juvenile crime rates. Other
causes of offensive acts include frustration or failure in school, the increased
of drugs and alcohol, and the growing
of child abuse and child neglect. All these conditions tend to increase the probability of a child committing a criminal act,
a direct causal relationship has not yet been established.

questions.analysis: centering 【线索】与下一句 "focusing on the role of society" 形成结构对照 线索就在同段下一句 Theories focusing on the role of society suggest that children commit crimes in __(4)__ to their failure…。两句结构完全平行：Theories ___ on X suggest that…，因此 ___ 必须与 focusing 同义，意为 "聚焦于、以…为中心"。这一同段 【选项】A) acting ✗ 搭配偏向 "行动/扮演"，与 focus 含义不一致 acting 与 on 搭配多表示 "对…采取行动" 或 "按照…行事"，与平行句 focusing on the role of society 的 "聚焦于" 之意不对应。 B) relying ✗ 义为 "依赖"，与 "聚焦" 错位 relying on 表 "依赖于"，意味着把个体当作工具或依据，与下一句 focusing on the role of C) centering ✓ center on = focus on，与平行句精确对应 center on 是 "以…为中心、聚焦于…" 的固定表达，直接对应下一句 Theories focusing on the role of society 中的 focusing on，使两类理论的并列论述结构成立。 D) commenting ✗ 义为 "评论"，色彩过轻且与平行项不一致 focusing on 的对照不成立。 【验证】代回原句：Theories __(1)__ on the individual suggest that children engage in criminal behavior… → Theories centering on the individual suggest that…，与下一句 Theories focusing on the role of society suggest that… 形成 "以个体 vs 以社会为焦点" 的并列论

because 【线索】本句内 "个人理论" 的因果指向：惩罚不足 → 犯罪 线索就在空格前后：Theories __(1)__ on the individual suggest that children engage in criminal behavior __(2)__ they were not sufficiently penalized for previous misdeeds 【选项】A) before ✗ 时间先后，无法表达因果 B) unless ✗ 条件反向，会颠倒因果方向 C) until ✗ 时间持续关系，不构成原因解释 D) because ✓ 原因连词，精准对应该理论的因果机制 罪的因果机制；且与同句后半句 or that they have learned criminal behavior through __(3)__ 【验证】代回：children engage in criminal behavior __(2)__ they were not sufficiently penalized for previous misdeeds → because they were not sufficiently penalized…， 与后续 or that they have learned… 形成 "原因 A 或 原因 B" 的并列，与 outline 中 "个体

interaction 【线索】本句已点明 "通过…与他人 learn behavior"，强调日常往来 线索在本句：they have learned criminal behavior through __(3)__ with others。"通过 的 because they were not sufficiently penalized 是与之并列的另一种成因，说明本句是 经典的 "模仿学习" 视角——日常 interaction 是其前提。 【选项】 A) interaction ✓ 中性、双向的 "互动"，完美承载 "与他人接触习得行为" B) assimilation ✗ 义为 "同化"，方向单一且语义过重 C) cooperation ✗ 义为 "合作"，色彩与犯罪习得场景不符 D) consultation ✗ 义为 "咨询"，语义过窄 【验证】代回：they have learned criminal behavior through __(3)__ with others → through interaction with others，呼应同段开头 Theories __(1)__ on the individual suggest that… 的 "个体焦点理论"，承接 "模仿/习得" 经典视角，与 outline 中 "两类经典理论之个

response 【线索】上下文是 "以社会为焦点" 的理论给出 "因→果" 解释 线索见 Theories focusing on the role of society suggest that children commit crimes in __(4)__ to their failure to rise above their socioeconomic status——"未能突破自身 社会经济地位" 是因，"实施犯罪" 是果；空格要表达的就是 "对…的反应"。in response to 【选项】A) return ✗ in return for 才常用，与本句 to 不匹配 return 的常见搭配是 in return for（作为对…的回报），且 "回报" 与 "因挫败而犯罪" 的语境 B) reply ✗ 意为 "答复"，多用于对话/信件场景 to your letter 之类。 C) reference ✗ in reference to = 关于，与因果不搭 reference 的固定搭配 in reference to 意为 "关于、提及"，仅表话题指向，无法表达 "对挫败的反 D) response ✓ in response to 是 "作为对…的反应" 的固定表达 response 与 in / to 构成 in response to，正是 "作为对（挫败）的反应" 这一标准说法，精确 【验证】代回：children commit crimes in __(4)__ to their failure to rise above their socioeconomic status → in response to their failure…，与社会焦点理论 "挫败 → 犯罪

or 【线索】前后是 "社会焦点理论" 给出的两种并列解释，可同时成立 线索见 children commit crimes in __(4)__ to their failure to rise above their socioeconomic status, __(5)__ as a rejection of middle-class values——"对挫败的反应" 【选项】 A) or ✓ 并列连接两种解释，符合 "也可以理解为…" B) but rather ✗ 需先有否定才能 "而是"，结构不成立 C) but ✗ 转折语义不符两种解释并存 D) or else ✗ 表 "否则将…"，语义错位 or else 通常用于警告 "否则会有…后果"（do X, or else…），与本句陈述两种并列原因的语境完全 【验证】代回：in __(4)__ to their failure to rise above their socioeconomic status, __(5)__ as a rejection of middle-class values → in response to their failure…, or as a rejection of middle-class values，前后两种平行解释自洽共存，与 outline 中 "社会焦点理论" 列举多

ignoring 【线索】主句聚焦弱势家庭，但事实是富裕家庭也犯罪，隐含转折 线索在本句：Most theories…have focused on children from disadvantaged families, __(6)__ the fact that children from wealthy homes also commit crimes.——前半句说 【选项】A) considering ✗ 意为 "考虑"，与主句 "只关注弱势" 矛盾 focused on…disadvantaged families"，两者自相矛盾。 B) ignoring ✓ "忽视" 完美对应理论盲区 C) highlighting ✗ 义为 "突出"，与盲区指控相反 D) discarding ✗ 义为 "丢弃"，对象错配且语气过重 discarding 意为 "抛弃、丢弃"，多用于丢弃物品/想法，对 "事实" 而言通常用 ignore；且语气过 【验证】代回：Most theories…have focused on children from disadvantaged families, __(6)__ the fact that children from wealthy homes also commit crimes. → ignoring the fact

for 【线索】前是 "犯罪行为"，后是 "管教缺失"，关系是 "出于…原因" 线索见本句 The latter may commit crimes __(7)__ lack of adequate parental control. ——commit crimes 是结果，lack of adequate parental control 是原因。表达 "出于…原 因/由于…" 的常用介词是 for（do something for some reason）。 【选项】A) on ✗ on 多表 "基于/在…之上"，不与 lack 配做原因 on 在表 "原因" 时多见于 act on impulse，与 commit crimes on lack of… 搭配不成立。 B) in ✗ in lack of 不是地道搭配，原因关系不通 in 用在 in need of / in want of 这类固定短语，但 in lack of 并非英语固定搭配，且表达不出 "出 C) for ✓ for 表 "出于…原因"，与 lack of … 自然连用 for 表 "由于、出于"，commit crimes for lack of adequate parental control 即 "由于管教不 D) with ✗ with 表 "伴随/凭借"，无法表达 "由于…" 【验证】代回：The latter may commit crimes __(7)__ lack of adequate parental control. → for lack of adequate parental control，因果明确，且承接前句 "富裕家庭孩子也犯罪" 的原因

subject 【线索】前半句 tentative 已奠定 "未定论、可被挑战" 的基调 线索就在本句前半：All theories, however, are tentative and are __(8)__ to criticism. ——并列连接词 and 要求空格语义与前半 tentative（暂定的、不确定的）同向。tentative criticism 正是 "易遭批评" 的固定说法。 【选项】A) immune ✗ be immune to = "对…免疫"，方向与 tentative 相反 immune 表 "免疫、不受影响"，若代入则成为 "理论免受批评"，与前半 tentative "还很初步" 完 B) resistant ✗ be resistant to = "抗…"，方向同样相反 resistant 表 "抵抗、不易受影响"，与 "暂定、待考" 的逻辑同样不一致。 C) sensitive ✗ be sensitive to 多表情绪/感官反应，对象错配 D) subject ✓ be subject to criticism = "易受批评"，精准对应 tentative subject 与 to 构成 be subject to，意为 "易受…、有待…"，be subject to criticism 即 "易遭批 评、不能免于批评"，与 tentative 同向，自然衔接。 【验证】代回：All theories, however, are tentative and are __(8)__ to criticism. → are tentative and are subject to criticism，与 outline 中 "第二段承认所有理论都有局限" 的谨慎收束完

affect 【线索】下一句给出具体路径，说明只是 "影响"，并非 "减少" 或 "反映" 线索见紧接的下一句 For example, changes in the economy that __(10)__ to fewer job opportunities for youth and rising unemployment __(11)__ make gainful employment increasingly difficult to obtain.——这是举例说明 "社会结构变化如何通 词 affect（影响）来概括，不能是 reduce（减少，方向反了）或 reflect（反映，主客 倒置）。 【选项】 A) affect ✓ 中性 "影响"，可被 indirectly 自然修饰 B) reduce ✗ 意为 "降低"，与下文 "导致犯罪上升" 相反 C) chock ✗ 拼写本身不构成 "影响/抑制" 的动词义 D) reflect ✗ 意为 "反映"，主客关系反了 【验证】代回：Changes in the social structure may indirectly __(9)__ juvenile crime rates. → may indirectly affect juvenile crime rates，承接下文 "通过经济传导链" 的具体例子，与

lead 【线索】to 后是 "工作机会减少 + 失业上升"，明显为 "结果" 线索在本句：changes in the economy that __(10)__ to fewer job opportunities for youth and rising unemployment——"工作机会减少和失业上升" 是因果链中的 "结果"， 因此 ___ to 必须是 "导致" 的意思。lead to 是表 "导致" 的最标准短语。 【选项】A) point ✗ point to = "指向/暗示"，并非 "造成" B) lead ✓ lead to = "导致"，最标准的因果短语 C) come ✗ come to 偏 "达到/合计"，不表造成结果 D) amount ✗ amount to = "总额为/相当于"，语义错位 【验证】代回：changes in the economy that __(10)__ to fewer job opportunities for youth and rising unemployment → that lead to fewer job opportunities…，符合 outline 中

in general 【线索】上文给出经济传导链，本句作普遍性结论而非对比/数据 线索见上下文 For example, changes in the economy that __(10)__ to fewer job opportunities for youth and rising unemployment __(11)__ make gainful employment increasingly difficult to obtain.——前面已铺好 "经济变化→工作机会少 【选项】 A) in general ✓ "总体而言"，承接经济变化对就业的普遍后果 B) on average ✗ 需有数据均值语境，本句无数据 C) by contrast ✗ 对比无对象，逻辑断裂 D) at length ✗ "详尽地/最终"，与一句话总结的语气不符 【验证】代回：rising unemployment __(11)__ make gainful employment increasingly difficult to obtain → rising unemployment in general make gainful employment…，对前述经

turn 【线索】上文给出 "经济差→不满"，本句续接 "不满→犯罪"，构成连锁反应 线索遍布第三段：changes in the economy that __(10)__ to fewer job opportunities for youth and rising unemployment __(11)__ make gainful employment increasingly difficult to obtain. The resulting discontent may in __(12)__ lead more youths into criminal behavior.——"经济变化 → 失业 → 不满 → 犯罪" 是一连串依次触发的因果链， 【选项】A) case ✗ in case = "以防/万一"，与因果链不符 B) short ✗ in short = "简言之"，本句不是总结 C) turn ✓ in turn = "反过来/依次"，精准承载链式因果 turn 与 in 构成 in turn，意为 "反过来又/依次"，与上文 "经济→失业→不满" 接续 "不满→犯罪" D) essence ✗ in essence = "本质上"，语气与链式承接不符 【验证】代回：The resulting discontent may in __(12)__ lead more youths into criminal behavior. → may in turn lead more youths into criminal behavior，与 outline 中 "第

experienced 【线索】下一句给出 "单亲、双职工" 这些社会变迁现象，是被动承受而非主动发起 线索见 More families consist of one-parent households or two working parents; __(14)__, children are likely to have less supervision at home __(15)__ was common in the traditional family __(16)__.——这些是社会层面的客观变化，对家庭而言是被动承受 "经历" 而非主动 "承担" 或 "幸存"。因此应填 experienced。 【选项】A) survived ✗ 意为 "幸存"，语义过重且对象错配 survived 表 "从…中幸存"，多用于灾难/危机，搭配 changes 不合习惯，且语义过重。 B) noticed ✗ 意为 "注意到"，主体应为感知者，家庭难以 notice 变化 noticed 表 "注意到"，主语通常是人或观察者，家庭整体作为承载单位 notice changes 不合 C) undertaken ✗ 意为 "承担/着手"，要求家庭主动发起变化 D) experienced ✓ "经历" 是承载社会变化的标准用语 【验证】代回：Families have also __(13)__ changes these years. → Families have also experienced changes these years.，与下一句单亲/双职工的具体变化举例一致，与 outline 中 "第四段：家庭变化" 自洽。

consequently 【线索】前句是家庭结构变化，后句是其后果（监护减少），明显因果 线索就在前后两句的语义关系：前句 More families consist of one-parent households or two working parents 描述家庭结构变化为单亲/双职工，后句 children are likely to have less supervision at home 说明 "孩子在家所受监护减少"——后者是前者直接导致的 【选项】A) contrarily ✗ 意为 "相反地"，前后并无对立 B) consequently ✓ "因此"，恰好引出家庭结构变化的后果 C) similarly ✗ "类似地" 需有可比的两类现象 D) simultaneously ✗ "同时" 仅表时间并行，缺因果 【验证】代回：More families consist of one-parent households or two working parents; __(14)__, children are likely to have less supervision at home… → ; consequently, children are likely to have less supervision…，前因后果逻辑严密，与 outline 中 "家庭

than 【线索】空前 less supervision 已锁死 than 比较 线索就在空前的关键词：children are likely to have less supervision at home __(15)__ was common in the traditional family __(16)__.——less 是比较级的标志，紧接其后的连 【选项】 A) than ✓ less … than … 比较结构的固定连词 than 与前文 less supervision 共同构成 "比……更少的监护" 比较结构，是该句法的唯一合法 B) that ✗ 无法引导比较级所需的对象从句 C) which ✗ 关系代词，不能用于比较结构 D) as ✗ as 用于 as … as 同等比较，不与 less 搭 as 用于 as much / as many 等同等比较结构，无法承接 less + 名词 这一不等比较。 【验证】代回：less supervision at home __(15)__ was common in the traditional family __(16)__ → less supervision at home than was common…，比较结构清晰、合法，承接

structure 【线索】上下文反复在谈 "家庭结构变化"，包括同段开头一句的潜台词 线索见同段一开头 Families have also __(13)__ changes these years. More families consist of one-parent households or two working parents——同段从一开始就在讨论 "家庭由什么组成、结构如何变化"，因此 traditional family ___ 应是 traditional family structure（传统家庭结构），与全段主题词 "结构" 一致。 【选项】A) system ✗ 意为 "系统"，过宽且偏制度化 system 指 "系统、体制"，传统家庭 system 偏向制度安排，不及 structure 直接对应 "家庭组成 形式"。 B) structure ✓ "结构" 精准对应 "家庭组成形式" structure 指 "结构"，traditional family structure 即 "传统家庭结构"，精准呼应同段开头 More families consist of one-parent households or two working parents 提到的家庭组成 C) concept ✗ "概念" 偏抽象观念，对象错位 D) heritage ✗ "遗产" 含正向文化色彩，与中性结构描述不符 【验证】代回：less supervision at home __(15)__ was common in the traditional family __(16)__. → than was common in the traditional family structure，与全段反复出现的

identifiable 【线索】include 之后给出三条具体原因，正是 "可辨识" 之意 线索见本句中 include 后罗列的三条具体原因：include frustration or failure in school, the increased __(18)__ of drugs and alcohol, and the growing __(19)__ of child abuse 认" 的范畴，所以 causes 的修饰语只能是 identifiable。 【选项】A) assessable ✗ "可评估的"，强调量化评估，对象错配 assessable 指 "可评估的"，常用于税项、风险量化，搭配 causes 偏离常用语境，且不及 identifiable 直接表 "可被辨识"。 B) identifiable ✓ "可识别的"，精准呼应后续具体清单 identifiable 表 "可识别、可辨认的"，与 include 后罗列的三条具体原因正好对应——既已能被 C) negligible ✗ "可忽略的"，与作者郑重列举矛盾 D) incredible ✗ "难以置信的"，色彩夸张且不贴学术语境 【验证】代回：Other __(17)__ causes of offensive acts include frustration or failure in school… → Other identifiable causes…，作者郑重列出三条 "可识别" 的额外成因，与 outline 中

incidence 【线索】三项并列原因均为 "现象增多→犯罪诱因"，要求与前两项对称 线索仍在本句的并列结构：include frustration or failure in school, the increased __(18)__ of drugs and alcohol, and the growing __(19)__ of child abuse and child 【选项】 A) incidence ✓ "发生率"，精确表达虐童疏忽案例增加 incidence 指 "发生率、发生频率"，the growing incidence of child abuse and child neglect B) awareness ✗ "意识"，awareness 上升应降低而非增加犯罪 C) exposure ✗ "曝光/暴露"，焦点是被报道，不是事件本身增多 D) popularity ✗ "流行、受欢迎"，色彩荒谬 【验证】代回：the growing __(19)__ of child abuse and child neglect → the growing incidence of child abuse and child neglect，与前一项 availability 平行对称，承接全段

sections.title: 阅读理解
sections.directions: Read the following four texts. Answer the questions after each text by choosing A, B, C or D. Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (40 points)

blocks.content: Hunting for a job late last year, lawyer Gant Redmon stumbled across CareerBuilder, a job database on the Internet. He searched it with no success but was attracted by the site's "personal search agent". It's an interactive feature that lets visitors key in job criteria such as location, title, and salary, then E-mails them when a matching position is posted in the database. Redmon chose the keywords legal, intellectual property and Washington, D.C. Three weeks later, he got his first notification of an opening. "I struck gold," says Redmon, who E-mailed his resume to the employer and won a position as in-house counsel for a company. With thousands of career-related sites on the Internet, finding promising openings can be time-consuming and inefficient. Search agents reduce the need for repeated visits to the databases. But although a search agent worked for Redmon, career experts see drawbacks. Narrowing your criteria, for example, may work against you: "Every time you answer a question you eliminate a possibility," says one expert. For any job search, you should start with a narrow concept—what you think you want to do—then broaden it. "None of these programs do that," says another expert. "There's no career counseling implicit in all of this." Instead, the best strategy is to use the agent as a kind of tip service to keep abreast of jobs in a particular database; when you get E-mail, consider it a reminder to check the database again. "I would not rely on agents for finding everything that is added to a database that might interest me," says the author of a job-searching guide. Some sites design their agents to tempt job hunters to return. When CareerSite's agent sends out messages to those who have signed up for its service, for example, it includes only three potential jobs—those it considers the best matches. There may be more matches in the database; job hunters will have to visit the site again to find them—and they do. "On the day after we send our messages, we see a sharp increase in our traffic," says Seth Peets, vice president of marketing for CareerSite. Even those who aren't hunting for jobs may find search agents worthwhile. Some use them to keep a close watch on the demand for their line of work or gather information on compensation to arm themselves when negotiating for a raise. Although happily employed, Redmon maintains his agent at CareerBuilder. "You always keep your eyes open," he says. Working with a personal search agent means having another set of eyes looking out for you.

Over the past century, all kinds of unfairness and discrimination have been condemned or made illegal. But one insidious form continues to thrive: alphabetism. This, for those as yet unaware of such a disadvantage, refers to discrimination against those whose surnames begin with a letter in the lower half of the alphabet. It has long been known that a taxi firm called AAAA cars has a big advantage over Zodiac cars when customers thumb through their phone directories. Less well known is the advantage that Adam Abbott has in life over Zoë Zysman. English names are fairly evenly spread between the halves of the alphabet. Yet a suspiciously large number of top people have surnames beginning with letters between A and K. Thus the American president and vice-president have surnames starting with B and C respectively; and 26 of George Bush's predecessors (including his father) had surnames in the first half of the alphabet against just 16 in the second half. Even more striking, six of the seven heads of government of the G7 rich countries are alphabetically advantaged (Berlusconi, Blair, Bush, Chirac, Chrétien and Koizumi). The world's three top central bankers (Greenspan, Duisenberg and Hayami) are all close to the top of the alphabet, even if one of them really uses Japanese characters. As are the world's five richest men (Gates, Buffett, Allen, Ellison and Albrecht). Can this merely be coincidence? One theory, dreamt up in all the spare time enjoyed by the alphabetically disadvantaged, is that the rot sets in early. At the start of the first year in infant school, teachers seat pupils alphabetically from the front, to make it easier to remember their names. So short-sighted Zysman junior gets stuck in the back row, and is rarely asked the improving questions posed by those insensitive teachers. At the time the alphabetically disadvantaged may think they have had a lucky escape. Yet the result may be worse qualifications, because they get less individual attention, as well as less confidence in speaking publicly. The humiliation continues. At university graduation ceremonies, the ABCs proudly get their awards first; by the time they reach the Zysmans most people are literally having a ZZZ. Shortlists for job interviews, election ballot papers, lists of conference speakers and attendees: all tend to be drawn up alphabetically, and their recipients lose interest as they plough through them.

When it comes to the slowing economy, Ellen Spero isn't biting her nails just yet. But the 47-year-old manicurist isn't cutting, filing or polishing as many nails as she'd like to, either. Most of her clients spend $12 to $50 weekly, but last month two longtime customers suddenly stopped showing up. Spero blames the softening economy. "I'm a good economic indicator," she says. "I provide a service that people can do without when they're concerned about saving some dollars." So Spero is downscaling, shopping at middle-brow Dillard's department store near her suburban Cleveland home, instead of Neiman Marcus. "I don't know if other clients are going to abandon me, too," she says. Even before Alan Greenspan's admission that America's red-hot economy is cooling, lots of working folks had already seen signs of the slowdown themselves. From car dealerships to Gap outlets, sales have been lagging for months as shoppers temper their spending. For retailers, who last year took in 24 percent of their revenue between Thanksgiving and Christmas, the cautious approach is coming at a crucial time. Already, experts say, holiday sales are off 7 percent from last year's pace. But don't sound any alarms just yet. Consumers seem only mildly concerned, not panicked, and many say they remain optimistic about the economy's long-term prospects even as they do some modest belt-tightening. Consumers say they're not in despair because, despite the dreadful headlines, their own fortunes still feel pretty good. Home prices are holding steady in most regions. In Manhattan, "there's a new gold rush happening in the $4 million to $10 million range, predominantly fed by Wall Street bonuses," says broker Barbara Corcoran. In San Francisco, prices are still rising even as frenzied overbidding quiets. "Instead of 20 to 30 offers, now maybe you only get two or three," says John Tealdi, a Bay Area real-estate broker. And most folks still feel pretty comfortable about their ability to find and keep a job. Many folks see silver linings to this slowdown. Potential home buyers would cheer for lower interest rates. Employers wouldn't mind a few fewer bubbles in the job market. Many consumers seem to have been influenced by stock-market swings, which investors now view as a necessary ingredient to a sustained boom. Diners might see an upside, too. Getting a table at Manhattan's hot new Alain Ducasse restaurant used to be impossible. Not anymore. For that, Greenspan & Co. may still be worth toasting.

Americans today don't place a very high value on intellect. Our heroes are athletes, entertainers, and entrepreneurs, not scholars. Even our schools are where we send our children to get a practical education—not to pursue knowledge for the sake of knowledge. Symptoms of pervasive anti-intellectualism in our schools aren't difficult to find. "Schools have always been in a society where practical is more important than intellectual," says education writer Diane Ravitch. "Schools could be a counterbalance." Ravitch's latest book, Left Back: A Century of Failed School Reforms, traces the roots of anti-intellectualism in our schools, concluding they are anything but a counterbalance to the American distaste for intellectual pursuits. But they could and should be. Encouraging kids to reject the life of the mind leaves them vulnerable to exploitation and control. Without the ability to think critically, to defend their ideas and understand the ideas of others, they cannot fully participate in our democracy. Continuing along this path, says writer Earl Shorris, "We will become a second-rate country. We will have a less civil society." "Intellect is resented as a form of power or privilege," writes historian and professor Richard Hofstadter in Anti-intellectualism in American Life, a Pulitzer-Prize winning book on the roots of anti-intellectualism in US politics, religion, and education. From the beginning of our history, says Hofstadter, our democratic and populist urges have driven us to reject anything that smells of elitism. Practicality, common sense, and native intelligence have been considered more noble qualities than anything you could learn from a book. Ralph Waldo Emerson and other Transcendentalist philosophers thought schooling and rigorous book learning put unnatural restraints on children: "We are shut up in schools and college recitation rooms for 10 or 15 years and come out at last with a bellyful of words and do not know a thing." Mark Twain's Huckleberry Finn exemplified American anti-intellectualism. Its hero avoids being civilized—going to school and learning to read— so he can preserve his innate goodness. Intellect, according to Hofstadter, is different from native intelligence, a quality we reluctantly admire. Intellect is the critical, creative, and contemplative side of the mind. Intelligence seeks to grasp, manipulate, re- order, and adjust, while intellect examines, ponders, wonders, theorizes, criticizes, and imagines. School remains a place where intellect is mistrusted. Hofstadter says our country's educational system is in the grips of people who "joyfully and militantly proclaim their hostility to intellect and their eagerness to identify with children who show the least intellectual promise."

blocks.content: The relation of language and mind has interested philosophers for many centuries. (41)The Greeks assumed that the structure of language had some connection with the process of thought, which took root in Europe long before people realized how diverse languages could be. Only recently did linguists begin the serious study of languages that were very different from their own. Two anthropologist-linguists, Franz Boas and Edward Sapir, were pioneers in describing many native languages of North and South America during the first half of the twentieth century. (42)We are obliged to them because some of these languages have since vanished, as the peoples who spoke them died out or became assimilated and lost their native languages. Other linguists in the earlier part of this century, however, who were less eager to deal with bizarre data from "exotic" language, were not always so grateful. (43)The newly described languages were often so strikingly different from the well studied languages of Europe and Southeast Asia that some scholars even accused Boas and Sapir of fabricating their data. Native American languages are indeed different, so much so in fact that Navajo could be used by the US military as a code during World War II to send secret messages. Sapir's pupil, Benjamin Lee Whorf, continued the study of American Indian languages. (44)Being interested in the relationship of language and thought, Whorf developed the idea that the structure of language determines the structure of habitual thought in a society. He reasoned that because it is easier to formulate certain concepts and not others in a given language, the speakers of that language think along one track and not along another. (45)Whorf came to believe in a sort of linguistic determinism which, in its strongest form, states that language imprisons the mind, and that the grammatical patterns in a language can produce far-reaching consequences for the culture of a society. Later, this idea became known as the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, but this term is somewhat inappropriate. Although both Sapir and Whorf emphasized the diversity of languages, Sapir himself never explicitly supported the notion of linguistic determinism.
